_provenance.notes: Alaska marine mammals are deeply intertwined with fisheries — as predators competing for fish, as indicators of ecosystem health, and as subjects of federal protection that constrains fishing operations. The Cook Inlet beluga whale (critically endangered at 279 animals) depends primarily on Chinook salmon — the same fish depleted by the Yukon crisis. Steller sea lion (western DPS) declined 80% from 1976-2000, triggering major changes to pollock and cod fishing operations. The sequential megafaunal collapse hypothesis (Estes et al.) suggests that killer whale predation on sea otters — after depletion of larger prey like whales and sea lions — caused kelp forest collapse in the Aleutians.

cook_inlet_beluga_whale.primary_prey: Chinook salmon (primary), eulachon (secondary), saffron cod, tomcod
cook_inlet_beluga_whale.chinook_salmon_dependency: Cook Inlet beluga whales are estimated to consume 1,500-2,000 Chinook salmon per whale per year. With 279 animals, the population requires 420,000-560,000 Chinook salmon annually.
threats: Chinook salmon prey depletion — Cook Inlet Chinook below escapement goals multiple years
Habitat loss — port construction, industrial development in Upper Cook Inlet
Vessel strikes — commercial and recreational boats in congested waterway
Climate change — warming water affecting prey distribution
Toxic contaminants — PCBs, PBDEs concentrated in Upper Cook Inlet
cook_inlet_beluga_whale.recovery_projection: NOAA recovery plan (2016): population unlikely to recover to historical levels (1,200+) before 2100. Current trajectory: potential extinction within 50 years without major intervention.

subsistence_hunt_history.1999: NOAA restricts subsistence hunt to 5 per year due to population decline
subsistence_hunt_history.2005: Hunt further restricted — population not responding
subsistence_hunt_history.current: Limited traditional harvest permitted: 1-2 per year for cultural continuity

steller_sea_lion_western_dps.esa_status: Endangered (western DPS delisted 2013 for eastern, western still listed)
steller_sea_lion_western_dps.status_note: Western DPS (west of 144°W) — Endangered. Eastern DPS — delisted 2013.

population_trend.notes: NOAA. Dramatic decline ongoing — ESA listed 1990.
NOAA. 80% decline from 1976 peak — among worst marine mammal declines in US history.

fisheries_restrictions_imposed: Critical habitat designated around Steller sea lion rookeries and haulouts
Pollock, Pacific cod, Atka mackerel fisheries restricted within 3nm and 10nm of rookeries
Junk food hypothesis: pollock is nutritionally inferior prey — prompted major NOAA research
AFA (1998) fishing season restrictions around SSL rookeries
steller_sea_lion_western_dps.cause_of_decline: Multiple hypotheses debated: commercial fishing of prey species (pollock, cod), climate change reducing prey quality, killer whale predation increase, disease. No single cause confirmed. Current consensus: multi-factor.

population_trend_southwest_alaska.notes: USGS survey. Near historical high for post-fur-trade era.

sea_otter.aleutian_kelp_connection: Estes et al. (1998, Science) documented that killer whale predation on sea otters — after depletion of larger prey — caused sea urchin population explosion, which then grazed kelp forests to bare rock across 25,000 km² of the Aleutian Islands.
sea_otter.trophic_cascade: Sea otter → sea urchin → kelp forest ecosystem. When otter numbers fall, urchins increase, kelp disappears. Kelp supports juvenile fish, nearshore species.
sea_otter.fisheries_interaction: Alaska Native subsistence hunting of sea otters permitted. Otters compete with shellfish fishermen for sea urchin, crab, and clam resources.

harbor_seals.trend: Stable in SE Alaska; declining in Gulf of Alaska
harbor_seals.exxon_valdez_impact: 300 harbor seals killed immediately in PWS (1989). ADF&G documented elevated contaminant levels in PWS seals for 15+ years post-spill.

killer_whale_resident_pods.ak_j_k_l_pods_status: Southern Resident killer whales (WA/BC) ESA Endangered — Alaska transient resident pods not listed
killer_whale_resident_pods.prey: Resident orcas: primarily Chinook salmon. Transient orcas: marine mammals.
killer_whale_resident_pods.chinook_connection: Southern Resident killer whales' primary prey is Chinook salmon from the Columbia River and SEAK runs. Their decline is directly linked to Chinook depletion.
